message:
QUESTION:
Did the 1 June move to a new content delivery network (CDN) improve the site's conversion rate, and what is a faster site worth?

DATA:
An online retailer migrated its website to a new content delivery network (CDN) on 1 June. Two weeks before (18-31 May) vs two weeks after (1-14 June):

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June |
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 |
| Median page load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s |
| 95th-percentile page load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% |

Conversion = orders / sessions. Page load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views.

Same two calendar periods last year, when there were no site or infrastructure changes: conversion 2.4% (18-31 May) and 2.6% (1-14 June).

The retailer's conversion rate rises every year in early June when the summer ranges launch. This year the summer ranges again launched on 1 June. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.

Here is a draft analysis:

<analysis>
**CDN migration: performance and conversion impact**

**Background.** The site moved to a new CDN on 1 June. This note compares the two weeks before the migration (18-31 May) with the two weeks after (1-14 June). Load times come from real-user monitoring, so they reflect what customers experienced on their own devices and connections. The analysis uses site-wide totals; device and channel splits are not included.

**Speed.** The migration delivered a large improvement in page speed. Median page load time fell from 3.2 seconds to 2.1 seconds, a 34% reduction. The slowest experiences improved even more: the 95th-percentile load time fell from 7.5 to 4.8 seconds, so the 95th-percentile load time fell by 56%. This matters because the slowest page loads are the ones most likely to drive customers away. Median load time is now 2.1 seconds, and 95% of page loads complete within 4.8 seconds.

**Engagement.** Bounce rate fell by a third, from 48% to 32%, indicating that far fewer visitors are leaving after a single page (bounce rate is the share of sessions that view only one page). Sessions also grew, from 200,000 to 210,000 (5%), and orders from 5,000 to 5,670 (13%).

**Conversion.** Conversion rose from 2.50% (5,000 orders from 200,000 sessions) to 2.70% (5,670 from 210,000), a gain of 0.2 points that we attribute to the faster site. No other site changes were made in the period, so the CDN is the only candidate explanation on the site side. In relative terms the gain is 8%, and at current volumes it is worth roughly 420 extra orders a fortnight (0.2% of 210,000 sessions). Orders per day rose from about 357 to 405.

**What is a second worth?** Median load time fell by 1.1 seconds and conversion rose by 0.2 points, so each second of load time is worth about 0.18 points of conversion, and a further one-second improvement would add another 0.18 points. This gives us a simple rule for prioritising future performance work against other projects.

**Next steps.**
1. Prioritise further speed work, starting with image optimisation on product pages, with a target of a 1.1-second median load time.
2. Use the 0.18-points-per-second figure in business cases for performance projects.
3. Continue monitoring load times and conversion weekly. Two weeks is a short window, and we should confirm that the speed improvement holds as traffic grows over the summer.

**Conclusion.** The CDN migration made the site substantially faster and lifted conversion by 0.2 points.
</analysis>

Produce an improved version.
response:
# CDN migration: performance and conversion impact

## Summary

The new CDN made the site substantially faster. Median page load time fell by about a third, and the slowest page loads improved by a similar proportion. The rise in conversion over the same period, however, cannot be credited to the CDN. Conversion rose by 0.2 points, from 2.50% to 2.70%. It rose by exactly the same amount over the same calendar weeks last year (2.4% to 2.6%), when nothing on the site changed. In both years the summer ranges launched on 1 June. Once that seasonal lift is allowed for, the estimated effect of the CDN on conversion is about zero.

These data therefore cannot tell us what a faster site is worth. We need a controlled test to answer that question.

## Speed

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s | −1.1 s (−34%) |
| 95th-percentile load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s | −2.7 s (−36%) |

Load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views. They reflect what customers experienced on their own devices and connections. The slowest page loads improved slightly more than the typical one, in relative terms. Half of page loads now complete within 2.1 seconds, and 95% within 4.8 seconds.

The improvement is large, and the timing fits the migration. The summer launch would not be expected to make pages load faster. If anything, higher traffic tends to slow a site down.

## Engagement and volume

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 | +5% |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 | +13% |
| Orders per day | ~357 | ~405 | +13% |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% | −4 points (−8% relative) |

Bounce rate is the share of sessions that view only one page. A faster site could explain the fall in bounce rate. So could the summer launch, since new ranges give visitors more reasons to browse. We do not have last year's bounce rate for the same weeks, so we cannot separate the two causes.

## Conversion

| | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| This year (new CDN from 1 June) | 2.50% | 2.70% | +0.20 points |
| Last year (no site changes) | 2.4% | 2.6% | +0.2 points |
| **Difference (estimated CDN effect)** | | | **≈ 0 points** |

In relative terms the seasonal lift was about 8% in both years: 8.3% last year and 8.0% this year. The summer range launch alone is enough to explain the whole of this year's increase.

It is true that the CDN was the only *site* change in the period. It was not the only change, though, because the summer launch happened on the same day. A simple before/after comparison cannot separate the two. The draft attributed the full 0.2 points to the CDN, along with the 420 extra orders a fortnight that follow from it. That was not justified.

**Precision.** Two weeks of data per period is short. Treating sessions as independent, the sampling error on this year's 0.2-point rise is about ±0.1 points (95% interval). Comparing against last year roughly doubles that uncertainty, and day-to-day swings add more. A single year is also a weak guide to the "normal" seasonal lift, because the size of the summer launch varies from year to year. A modest CDN effect could be hiding inside the noise in either direction. The honest conclusion is that there is **no detectable conversion effect**, which is not the same as proof of no effect.

## What is a second worth?

These data do not support a per-second figure. The draft divided 0.2 points by 1.1 seconds to get 0.18 points per second. That calculation fails for three reasons:

1. **The 0.2 points is seasonal.** After removing the seasonal lift, the conversion change attributable to speed is about zero. That would give a value of about zero per second, which is also not a credible estimate.
2. **One before/after pair cannot reveal a rate.** We have a single change in speed and a single change in conversion. We cannot tell whether the relationship is linear or has diminishing returns. Going from 3.2 s to 2.1 s may matter quite differently from going from 2.1 s to 1.1 s.
3. **The choice of metric is arbitrary.** The 95th percentile improved by 2.7 seconds. Dividing by that instead would give a different "per-second" value from the same data.

## Next steps

1. **Run a controlled test to measure the value of speed.** For example, serve a randomly chosen share of traffic through a slower path, with a small amount of delay added. Alternatively, test a specific speed improvement on a random half of traffic. Either design removes seasonality and gives a defensible conversion effect per second.
2. **Use the real-user monitoring data within the post-migration period.** Compare conversion across sessions or segments with different load times, such as device types, regions and connection types. Control for traffic source and product category. This is weaker than a test but faster to produce. Segments where the CDN cut load times most could also be compared with those where it changed little.
3. **Do not use a points-per-second figure in business cases** until step 1 or step 2 produces one. Do not set a 1.1-second target on the grounds that it will add 0.18 points of conversion.
4. **Keep monitoring load times weekly through the summer** to confirm that the speed gains hold as traffic grows. Also pull last year's bounce rate and sessions for the same weeks, so that engagement can be adjusted for seasonality in the same way as conversion.
5. **Value the CDN on its other merits as well.** These include hosting and bandwidth costs, reliability, and search ranking. Those benefits do not depend on a measurable conversion lift.

## Conclusion

The CDN migration made the site about a third faster, at both the median and the 95th percentile. Conversion rose by 0.2 points, but it rose by the same amount at the same point last year because of the summer range launch. There is therefore no evidence yet that the faster site improved conversion. The value of a second of load time needs to be measured with a controlled test; it cannot be inferred from this before/after comparison.

---

**Corrections to the draft:**
- **95th-percentile reduction:** it was 36%, not 56%.
- **Bounce rate:** it fell from 48% to 44%, not to 32%. That is a 4-point fall, not "by a third".
- **Attribution:** the conversion rise was attributed to the CDN even though last year's identical seasonal rise shows otherwise.
- **The 420 extra orders and the 0.18 points per second:** both figures were dropped because they rest on that attribution.
- **The 1.1-second target:** it was also dropped, because it relied on extrapolating a straight line.
